reasons.C: Closest to Crothers' genial irony: short declaratives set against longer ones, epigrammatic turns ('that is what he is for', 'no secrets from us, for Dickens has no secrets'), and homely shop and household images used lightly rather than piled on.
reasons.B: Good whimsical close and domestic similes (crinoline, fire) in his manner, but 'laid on with a trowel' and the confessional first-person run feel slightly more modern-plain and less aphoristic than the passage.
reasons.A: Right mild self-deprecating stance and a wry last line, but sentences run long and even, with fewer of the quick witty inversions that drive the passage's rhythm.
reasons.D: Reads as a modern reviewer: second-person 'Suppose you', analytic framing ('curious consequence', 'pleasures of recognition rather than discovery') and a flat argumentative close, with little of the playful turn of phrase.
